title: 🎙️ Repair Culture & Practical Tech
description: Today is about things you can fix, keep running, and pass on — repair culture, right-to-repair wins and setbacks, gear that outlives its manufacturer's support window, and the maker ethos of building to last rather than building to replace. We're interested in tools, devices, and projects where longevity, repairability, and self-sufficiency intersect, especially in rural and off-grid contexts where you can't just run to a repair shop. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Repair Culture & Practical Tech' — the right to repair movement, gear that outlasts its manufacturer, DIY fixes, and tools built for longevity.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical conflict; natural disasters without an engineering or preparedness angle; wildlife and conservation; working-lands policy; Indigenous governance; science discoveries with no DIY or hardware relevance; financial market news.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Hands-on hardware journalism counts fully even without an explicit right-to-repair hook.
- 80-100: Directly about repairability — right-to-repair legislation wins and losses, iFixit-style teardowns scoring repairability, gear designed for user serviceability, products outliving manufacturer support and how owners keep them running, permacomputing, vintage hardware still in active use, open-source hardware, Rossmann-style repair advocacy, 3D-printed replacement parts, battery replacement guides, rural and off-grid repair self-sufficiency.
- 55-79: Hands-on maker and DIY content — builds, modifications, hardware hacks, workshop projects, practical electronics guides with real technical depth, 3D printing hardware and filament, off-grid and solar gear, home lab hardware, tools and workshop equipment, battery and power tech. Most genuine hands-on hardware journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Gadget and device reviews with some technical substance; consumer electronics touching software longevity or ecosystem lock-in; hardware whose selling point is open firmware or modular design.
- 10-29: Surface-level product announcements, gadget speculation, leaked specs, general tech news with no hardware or repair angle.

ANCHORS: 'Framework Laptop 16 teardown: a 9/10 repairability score' → 98. 'Oregon's right-to-repair law takes effect' → 92. 'Building a solar-powered Raspberry Pi weather station' → 68. 'Samsung teases thinner bezels on next Galaxy' → 15.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Kagi Small Web] Luke Mitchell on Design Process
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Tell us a little bit about yourself

I have been a designer of one sort or another since 2011. I started out as a Graphic Designer who also built websites, but as I got more and more interested in web apps and websites I started moving towards digital design then product design.

I am currently Lead Product Designer at Definely. I am happy working on design at any step of the process, whether that be strategy, research, prototyping, testing, design systems, and everything in between.

I also love to code when I get the chance, I am a big fan of HTML and CSS, but I will give most languages a try.

What are the first questions you ask at the beginning of every project?

  • What research do we already have?
  • Has any design work already been done?
  • What resources do we have to share?
  • Where did this idea come from? (support ticket, stakeholders etc.)
  • How urgent is it? (should I drop other things I’m working on to start on this?)
  • Who is the team that will be working on it?

How do you approach pricing with clients? How did you arrive at this?

I’ve never been freelance or been directly involved in too many pricing conversations, but I often need to estimate how long things will take. I usually start with a broad estimate followed by frequent updates, I like to over estimate and then take anything ahead of schedule as a win.

What are the first things you do when you start a new project?

I don’t usually do anything concrete, and it depends on the project. But I will usually start by ask a bunch of questions, and then outline the next steps I will take. I will try and learn as much as I can about the problem, from there I see where the wind takes me and go from there.

What does your moodboarding process look like? Where do you source inspiration?

I don’t moodboard as often I as used to, but when I do my sources vary. I tend to avoid just moodboarding bits of UI/UX, as that has too much of a bias for solutions. Instead I try to find an eclectic mix of sources, my favourites include architecture, interior design, photography, typography, and physical product design.

I read a lot articles from blogs and sites I like via RSS, and I save visuals I find inspiring on Savee.

What’s your favourite part of the design process? Why?

Prototyping. It’s great to move fast and get something out of your head, then test it with people quickly. I would love to have a number on the amount of hours I’ve saved on circular discussions about features by just building a little thing and showing it to people, it clarifies and validates faster than any amount of meetings could.

Are there any parts of your process that go against received wisdom? Or common steps that you skip? Why?

There have been times where I followed the ‘double diamond’ process religiously, but more often than not I tend to let the process reveal itself as move along. It really depends on the feature or product, but I find you can often skip a super in-depth discovery process for something far less formal and time consuming.

Similarly I often find that having a long iterative process of design drafts doesn’t really lead anywhere productive, sometimes shifting focus too much into detail too early in a project. I prefer to research to confirm assumptions, and then iterate on a shipped feature instead of iterating before launching anything at all.

Less double diamond and more squiggly line.

Is there anything else you suspect is unique or unusual about your practice?

I create lots of diagrams, which I don’t see very often from designers, I see it more from engineers and developers: Information architecture, user flows, workflows, swimlanes, all sorts. I think that it helps to get information structured and out of my head without a UI early. It really helps to focus on all those little words and connections, when you aren’t biased by colours, layout typography etc.

If you collaborate with others (copywriters, illustrators, developers, etc): when do you bring them in? How do you handle project management?

Early and often, if they’re curious to get involved. It can be very helpful to have a small team involved throughout the whole process. There have been plenty of times where a developer has asked a key question during a research interview, or a product manager has noticed an early inefficiency in my thinking, that would not have been caught until we were much further along otherwise.

What’s been the most impactful change you’ve made to your process? Where did you hear about it?

Asking “stupid” questions. I have learnt so much by asking questions that should have an obvious answer, and avoided massive assumptions early on. For example say somebody I’ve never worked with before mentions a “customer”, I will ask “What does ‘customer’ mean?”. The answer is often far more nuanced and unexpected than you might think.

Unfortunately I can’t remember where or when I first started doing this.

What parts of the process are non-negotiables for you?

Honestly, I’m happy to skip any part if there is a good reason to do so. I often have strong opinions on validating assumptions, and prototyping, but even those can be ditched in some projects.

How do you organise design files?

I’m not very good at this. I will occasionally have a blitz and a tidy up when things get overwhelming inside Figma. But if I’m handing anything over I’ll usually create a page with the name of a Linear ticket, and send links to that out.

What does design hand-off look like for you?

It depends on what I’m designing, if it’s a little change all that needed is a quick comment or Slack message. But as things get more complex I will document more heavily and write specs as needed, I’m not a pixel-perfect kind of guy.

I will also have short calls with the team and present the design and answer questions as they come up, and then document that instead if the feature is particularly big. I will often get involved directly with front-end code also if it saves a developer putting up with me listing 50 ‘snags’ that I’d like fixed.

Looking back over the last 12 months, how do people find out about you?

I’m not much of a self-promoter, I get a fair bit of traffic to my website, especially the bookmarks page, but it’s not something I actively push or post about anywhere else. I’m lucky to only have had to look for work once or twice in the last 10 years, both times I applied for those jobs. If I were ever to go freelance I would have to be much more proactive.

What elements of the process create speed bumps or challenges? How do you get out of these ruts?

I find projects often get stuck in a discussion loop, or lose momentum when the task seems a bit too big. I try to break that loop by doing or building something demonstrable that everyone can see, critique, and plan against. It’s easier to say if something works or doesn’t, or if it’s too ambitious, if you can see and use it.

How do you make decisions?

There are lots of factors to take into account for decision-making: time, urgency, impact etc. If it’s a short-term, low-impact, urgent decision I usually use experience and intuition to get those out of the way quickly. I know that the decision I make there is probably reversible and I can iterate on it later.

The trickier ones are the decisions where I care much more about the outcome, usually because it has long-term impact that would be hard to reverse quickly. In those cases I have to make sure I am prepared to answer any questions that might counter my opinion, I also like to be prepared with resources to back my decision up. If I can’t justify my decision with anything more than “because I think it’s right”, then I haven’t done my job.

That being said I am surrounded by smart people who I listen to when making decisions, and while I will push back I will concede or compromise when others have similarly well prepared arguments to mine.

Favourite tool, resource or course?

Physical: A nice pen and a nice notebook.

Digital: Things by Cultured Code.

Where can people find out more about you, keep up to date, or work with you?

Checkout my website, there are some other links on there: interroban.gg

items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Bangladeshi complainants allege Rampal power station’s pollution and climate risks threaten the Sunderbans, a world heritage site

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.

Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.

items.title: [Kagi Small Web] Deploying LiteLLM on Kubernetes
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Introduction

I have access to LLM APIs from several different providers. I use Hermes for all kinds of tasks, and I do not want to edit the Hermes configuration every time I switch models. So I set up LiteLLM and put the models from those different providers behind one OpenAI-compatible API. Hermes only needs to be configured once. After that, when I want to switch the underlying model, I just change the model mapping in the LiteLLM admin UI.

I first got everything working locally and confirmed that the models could actually be called. Then I moved it to Kubernetes and connected PostgreSQL, Redis, Traefik, and ArgoCD. This post documents the full setup and a few problems I ran into along the way.

items.title: [Fast Company] Google is helping bring cutting-edge battery tech to an old West Virginia strip mine
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

For decades, a sprawling site in West Virginia was mined for coal, and part of the operation is still active. But on a 500-acre section abandoned 20 years ago, something new is taking shape: a clean-energy project pairing solar power with cutting-edge battery technology that could help renewables deliver electricity around the clock.

The $350 million project, called Mammoth Solar, will sell energy to Google, which has a goal to get to 24/7 carbon-free energy on every grid where it operates. It’s the first development where the tech giant will rely on zinc batteries, an emerging long-duration technology that can store electricity for 10 hours.

It’s the next step in the evolution of renewable energy. A decade ago, most solar and wind projects didn’t include batteries at all, says Jon Yoder, president and CEO of MN8 Energy, which partnered with Google to build and operate the new plant. “There was no economically viable way to store that power when the sun wasn’t shining or the wind wasn’t blowing,” he says.

A few years later, lithium-ion batteries became viable for short-term storage. They work well for storing electricity for about four hours, helping cover the evening spike in demand after the sun goes down. But using them to bridge longer gaps remains too expensive.

MN8 and Google researched new options for long-term storage that could be used along with lithium-ion batteries, and “ran literally dozens of different combinations of technologies to compare the functionality against the cost,” Yoder says.

Zinc stood out, he says, because the batteries have a relatively high round-trip efficiency, meaning the amount of electricity you get out for the amount that you put in. The zinc batteries, made by a company called Eos, also use sustainable materials and don’t pose a fire risk.

“We chose to support Eos’s batteries because the chemistry relies on Earth-abundant materials—zinc and bromine—and a more resilient supply chain than traditional lithium-based systems,” says Campbell Howe, advanced energy program manager at Google. 

“Additionally,” Howe says, “Eos’s manufacturing facility in Pennsylvania is already stood up, which will continue to support job growth and economic development in the Appalachian region.”

The project will break ground in 2027, with 86 megawatts of solar panels in place by 2028; 70 megawatts of lithium-ion storage will be added by 2029, followed by 10 megawatts of the zinc batteries in 2030.

The zinc technology is still a relatively small amount of the project. “Because this is relatively new technology and because we want to see how it performs in real-world situations over an extended period of time, we sized it in a way where the economic investment still is prudent even with the remaining risks that could be latent in the business model for the zinc,” Yoder says.

But it’s a meaningful amount, and it will let both MN8 and Google see how the zinc batteries perform, including their real-world efficiency, to help plan future projects.

As the lithium-ion batteries cover the evening, the new batteries can help cover more of the night. “We can serve those hours from, let’s say, 10 at night until 8 the next morning, when the sun is coming up again,” Yoder says.

Because the zinc batteries are a smaller piece of the development, the project isn’t yet designed to provide energy all the time, “but that’s the theory of where we’re headed,” he says. “These three technologies, in combination between solar, short duration, and long duration, move the needle much closer to the ability to serve power on a 24/7 basis.”

items.title: [Fast Company] Chevron confirms it will invest billions to expand operations in oil-rich Venezuela
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Oil giant Chevron confirmed that it will expand its operations in Venezuela, just days after President Donald Trump announced an ambitious deal to develop the nation’s oil reserves and give the Pentagon a stake in the profits.

Chevron, the only U.S. oil company that has a major presence in the country, said Wednesday that it has been assigned additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt, where the company has an established position. Joint venture plans include investing more than $7 billion over the next five years, more than doubling production to approximately 600,000 barrels a day compared with 2026.

“Chevron’s history in Venezuela spans more than a century, and our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country’s deep resource potential and its ability to compete for investment within our portfolio for decades,” CEO Mike Wirth said in a prepared statement. “With improved terms and additional acreage, we are strengthening a portfolio that we believe can deliver attractive low-cost oil growth, support energy supply and create differentiated long-term value.”

Venezuela holds the world’s largest proven reserves, totaling more than 303 billion barrels of crude oil, according to OPEC’s 2025 Annual Statistical Bulletin. Saudi Arabia is a distant second with 267 billion barrels.

The announcement comes a day after a U.S. official, who briefed reporters on the expected announcement, said that Chevron officials and Energy Secretary Chris Wright were expected to visit Venezuela on Wednesday when the new investment would be formally unveiled. The official spoke on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House for the call.

Chevron is the second-largest U.S. oil company and the only one with a major presence in Venezuela. It has had a presence in the country since 1923. Its joint ventures Petroindependencia and Petropiar, S.A. operate extra-heavy oil projects in the Orinoco Oil Belt, while Petroboscan, S.A. is located in the Zulia State in western Venezuela.

The White House confirmed on Monday that it is partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners as part of Trump ‘s push to tap into Venezuela’s oil industry.

The sweeping agreement has been met with skepticism from analysts who say it will take years to revive Venezuela’s oil industry, which is in disarray after years of neglect.

Energy experts also have questioned whether Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez has the legal authority to give the company 100-year rights over 17 oil fields with reserves of 65 billion barrels — and whether future Venezuelan or American administrations would overturn the agreement.

Trump has had his eyes on Venezuela’s oil since the capture of Nicolás Maduro, and his aides call it a path away from reliance on oil from the Middle East. Trump has been pressing to get U.S. businesses to restore a presence in the country, and suggested Monday that other oil companies were readying for business in Venezuela. “We have Exxon going in, we have Chevron going in. We have our big oil companies going in,” he said. Trump in January said he was inclined to leave Exxon out of Venezuela after CEO Darren Woods called the country “uninvestable.”

A spokesman for Exxon said Tuesday, however, that “nothing has changed” on the company’s position regarding Venezuela.

Asked about Chevron’s announcement during an interview on Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said, “No American firm knows how to operate in Venezuela better than Chevron.”

Bessent told Fox News Channel’s “Fox & Friends” that Trump is “creating assets for the American people” with the deal and that the arrangement “is going to push down oil prices, push up production” to benefit U.S. consumers and the Venezuelan economy.

Trump has said that the agreement with Venezuela would “substantially lower” gasoline prices in the U.S. However, experts have repeatedly warned that Venezuela’s dilapidated oil infrastructure will require years of restoration work and tens of billions of dollars to resuscitate.

Meanwhile, the national average price for a gallon of regular gasoline jumped overnight to $4.12, according to the motor club AAA. That’s 93 cents more than it cost at this point last year.

Associated Press writers Aamer Madhani and Collin Binkley contributed to this report.

—Michelle Chapman, AP Business Writer
